claims.text: A near-miss pair is the silent bug: the operator sets the documented name and nothing happens. Only strict token-subsequence pairs qualify, so OLLAMA_NUM_CTX and OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL are not accused of being the same variable spelled two ways.
claims.why: The code in lines 967-987 implements near-miss detection with token subsequence check (short[0] == long[0] and _is_subsequence(short, long)), and excludes exact matches and cases where both names are documented and read (alias pair). The example is illustrative and not tested.

claims.text: DARK requires unanimity on the default (every site reads it as off) plus at least one site with no fallback -- i.e. there is a code path that simply does not run unless an operator knows the name. A variable that is off at one site and defaulted at another is MIXED, never dark: the feature is reachable, the defaults just disagree, which the conflict list reports.
claims.why: The code in _reconcile (lines 1011-1027) sets dark = states == {'OFF'} and any(s.dark for s in real). The comment describes the exact logic: unanimous OFF and at least one dark site. MIXED state is set when states has more than one element.

claims.text: Two passes: every module is parsed before any default is resolved, so a default written as an imported constant is compared by VALUE. Comparing the source text instead reports `DEFAULT_HOST` and its own literal as a disagreement while missing DEEPSEEK_MODEL, where the values really differ.
claims.why: The code in analyse (lines 1031-1046) first iterates over sources to collect module info, then creates a _Resolver with collected info, then scans each module. This matches the described two-pass design.
